transcript.text: LG F4V5VYP0W says OE and the clothes are sat in water. I'm not opening the little door at the bottom because last time I did that it flooded the whole kitchen. What else can I do?

OE means the machine has not managed to drain within its allowed time. With water still in the drum, it will usually refuse to spin as well. You do not need to open the filter door and flood the kitchen. The most likely causes are a blockage in the filter/pump path, a kink or blockage in the drain hose or household waste pipe, then—less commonly—a faulty drain pump. 1. Switch off and unplug the machine. Check the grey drain hose along the back and where it enters the standpipe or sink waste. Straighten any kink or crushed section. If the sink or standpipe is backing up, the household waste plumbing may be blocked rather than the washer. 2. Then select a Drain/Spin programme and listen from outside the machine—do not remove any panels. A humming or straining noise points more towards a blockage or jammed pump; complete silence makes a pump, wiring or control fault more likely. 3. If you do decide to clear the filter, first remove as much water as possible without opening it: bail the drum out slowly with a jug into a bucket, or use a wet vacuum if you have one. Put towels and a shallow tray down, unplug the machine, then loosen the filter only a little at a time to drain any remaining water in controlled amounts. If the hose is clear and it hums but cannot shift water, the filter/pump area still needs clearing before assuming the pump needs replacement. If it is silent on Drain/Spin, or the filter cannot be safely accessed, an engineer is the sensible next step.

The machine was pushed right back against the wall and the hose was squashed behind it, so I've pulled it out and straightened it. I tried the drain/spin again and it drained a bit slower than normal, then showed OE again. The pump hums and I can hear a rattle now and then. I still don't want to unscrew that filter.

OE means the washer has exceeded its drain time. Straightening the crushed hose has helped, but the slow drain, humming and occasional rattle now make a partial blockage around the pump/filter area the leading possibility—often a coin, hair grip, button or lint. A pump beginning to jam is the next possibility. You do not have to open the filter yourself. 1. Switch the washer off and unplug it. Check where its drain hose enters the standpipe or sink waste. Run the tap into that waste point for a minute. If it backs up or drains slowly, the household plumbing needs clearing; the washer may be pumping but has nowhere to send the water.
2. If the waste drains freely and the hose is no longer crushed, the restriction is more likely in the filter/pump path. If you do not want to deal with the filter, book an appliance engineer rather than repeatedly running Drain/Spin. ” They can drain it in a controlled way and clear the pump path before deciding whether the drain pump needs replacing.
I ran the tap into the kitchen sink and it drains fine, no backing up. So what now?

The kitchen waste is not the problem. OE means the washer has not emptied within its allowed time; with the waste draining freely, the slow drain plus humming/rattle points most strongly to a partial blockage or object in the pump/filter path. A drain pump that is beginning to jam is the second possibility. Because the hose was crushed, it may have contributed, but straightening it has not fully cured the fault. Avoid repeatedly running Drain/Spin, as a blocked or struggling pump can overheat. As you do not want to open the filter—which is reasonable with water still in the drum—the practical next step is an appliance engineer. Ask them to drain the machine in a controlled way, clear the pump filter and accessible pump path, and only then assess whether the drain pump needs replacement. At this stage, do not order a pump: the humming and rattle can be caused by debris rather than a failed pump.
